newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Shine seen returning to Malaysian tin price.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shine seen returning to Malaysian tin price.

text.p: A weak ringgit and rising demand are putting the shine back into Malaysian tin, with the price of the metal seen touching 15 ringgit ($5.42) a kg soon, analysts said on Tuesday.
The spot price on the Kuala Lumpur Tin Market hit a seven-month high of 14.86 ringgit on Tuesday.
Trading volumes have also been substantial, at an average of around 185 tonnes daily in the past five trading days, said analysts.
They said the spot price could reach the psychological level of 15 ringgit a kg by the end of this week if the ringgit stayed weak against the U.S. dollar and current market sentiment prevailed.
The last time tin traded above the 15 ringgit level was in November 1996.
"It all depends on the ringgit now...we don't expect it to go down much further but if it stays soft, then there's the chance of it (tin) hitting 15 ringgit," said a metals analyst.
He said much also depended on the London Metal Exchange's (LME) three-month spot price for tin, which virtually determines the direction of the Kuala Lumpur market.
"If there is an improvement in the London market tonight, then 15 ringgit in KL is for sure tomorrow," said the analyst.
"Fundamentally, the Malaysian tin price should be at 18 ringgit but it's not, because of the speculation on the LME," he added.
Heavy selling of tin on the LME has triggered the metal's price in Malaysia, traders said. The local price fell to a 27-month low of 13.52 ringgit a kg on July 11.
However, a sharp fall of the ringgit since last month has prompted buyers in Malaysia to ignore movements on the LME altogether on certain days, said traders.
"A weak ringgit means Malaysian tin will be cheaper for overseas buyers and that has been the prime factor moving the market in the last month," said a trader.
On Tuesday, the ringgit fell to a new 42-month low of 2.7930 against the U.S. dollar, before recovering to around 2.7700 at 0900 GMT.

"It doesn't look like the ringgit is going to fall to 2.8 or below, so if it stays at the current level, and there's not much profit-taking (in tin), the (spot) price could rise steadily to 15 ringgit," said the trader.

Dealers said fundamentally the metal was growing strong in both the Malaysian and London markets. "We have seen a steady rise in the number of inquiries and this means demand is growing," said a tin dealer.
Malaysia, the world's largest producer of tin in the 1970s, is a minor producer today. Its highest output was 76,800 tonnes in 1972 while last year it mined 5,174 tonnes.
